Exam Details

The Hawaii Journey Worker Electrician examination is administered by PSI for the Hawaii Department of Commerce and Consumer Affairs, Professional and Vocational Licensing Division. Candidates are not allowed to register for the examination until the Board approves the application and sends an approval letter. The exam is computer-based and is scheduled through PSI after eligibility is issued.

The Hawaii Journey Worker Electrician exam contains 70 questions, allows 180 minutes of testing time, and lists a minimum passing score of 70%. The exam may also include a small number of unscored experimental questions used for examination development. These unscored questions do not count toward the final score.

The Journey Worker Electrician content outline includes 10 questions on General Electrical Knowledge, 10 questions on Service, Feeders, and Branch Circuits, 10 questions on Grounding and Bonding, 10 questions on Conductors and Cables, 6 questions on Raceways and Boxes, 6 questions on Special Occupancies, Conditions, and Equipment, 6 questions on Electrical Power, Motors, and Equipment for General Use, 4 questions on Low Voltage and Communication Circuits, 4 questions on Lighting, and 4 questions on Safety Information.

This exam outline shows why students should study across the full range of electrical topics. The largest areas include general electrical knowledge, services, feeders, branch circuits, grounding and bonding, conductors, and cables, but smaller categories still affect the final score. A candidate may need to identify a wiring rule, apply a grounding requirement, understand a service or feeder condition, answer a motor or equipment question, interpret a lighting requirement, or solve a calculation.

Because the test is timed, candidates should prepare for both speed and accuracy. Journey worker electrical exams reward students who can understand the question, identify the electrical subject, locate the proper code material, and apply the rule without spending too much time on one item. This combo supports that preparation by combining trade review, calculation practice, and NEC-based study.

Open Book Test

The Hawaii Journey Worker Electrician exam is an open book examination. The PSI candidate bulletin lists the examination as open book and states that the reference material is provided by the examination center. The listed reference material in the current bulletin is the National Electrical Code, 2020 edition.

This product is based on the 2026 NEC and includes the National Electrical Code 2026 Paperback for updated study, code navigation practice, and calculation-based preparation. Candidates should follow the current PSI and Hawaii Board testing instructions for the code edition and reference material used on exam day.

Open book testing still requires serious preparation. A code book is only helpful when the student knows how to use it. Candidates need to understand the subject being tested, locate the correct article or table, read the rule carefully, and apply the requirement under timed conditions. Slow reference navigation can make even familiar electrical topics difficult during an exam.

The National Electrical Code 2026 Paperback included in this combo gives students a physical code reference for building those skills during study. Students can practice locating common journeyman exam subjects such as conductor ampacity, services, feeders, branch circuits, grounding electrode systems, equipment grounding conductors, bonding jumpers, raceways, boxes, motors, electrical power, lighting, special occupancies, low-voltage circuits, communication circuits, and calculation-related provisions.

Open book study should include active NEC navigation. Students should use the index, article headings, definitions, tables, notes, and exceptions while answering practice-style questions. The goal is to become comfortable using the NEC as a working reference, not simply as a book to read from front to back. A student who regularly practices finding information is better prepared to manage time during a timed reference-based exam.

Licensing Steps

Hawaii Journey Worker Electrician candidates begin by meeting the experience and academic coursework requirements established by Hawaii law and the Board of Electricians and Plumbers. The applicant must document qualifying electrical experience and completion of the required electrical academic coursework before the Board can approve the application for examination.

The candidate submits the application for license to the Professional and Vocational Licensing Division with the required supporting documents. Experience verification must be completed and notarized by each licensed electrician under whom the applicant received experience or training. If experience was earned in a jurisdiction that does not require licensure as a journey worker, supervising, or master electrician and only requires a contractor license, the Board may accept a notarized experience verification form signed by the licensed contractor with verification of the contractor license.

The application must also include verification of completion of the required electrical academic coursework. Hawaii accepts documentation such as a diploma, certificate of completion, certificate of competence, certificate of achievement, transcript with completion information, a letter from the registrar of a University of Hawaii Community College, or a certificate of completion from an approved apprenticeship program when applicable.

After the Board reviews and approves the application, the candidate receives approval to register for the PSI examination. The candidate then schedules the exam through PSI, follows the computer-based testing procedures, and reports to the exam site with the required identification and testing documents.

After testing, the candidate receives score information according to PSI procedures. Passing the exam is part of the licensing process, but the license process is not complete until all Board requirements are satisfied. Candidates should follow the Professional and Vocational Licensing Division’s instructions for final licensing steps after examination.

A strong licensing plan begins early. Candidates should keep accurate employment records, obtain required notarized experience verification forms, complete the required academic coursework, review the exam outline, and build a study routine that includes trade review, calculation practice, and NEC navigation.

State Requirements

Hawaii requires a license before a person may act as a journey worker electrician, journey worker specialty electrician, supervising electrician, supervising specialty electrician, journey worker industrial electrician, supervising industrial electrician, or maintenance electrician. A person may not hold themselves out as an electrician without the proper license under Hawaii’s electrician licensing law.

For the Journey Worker Electrician license, Hawaii requires the applicant to be at least 18 years old and provide satisfactory evidence of experience in residential or commercial wiring of at least 5 years full-time or its equivalent, but not less than 10,000 hours, in the trade under the supervision of a journey worker or supervising electrician.

Hawaii also requires satisfactory completion of 240 hours of electrical academic coursework accepted by a University of Hawaii Community College offering an appropriate program of study. This academic coursework requirement applies to journey worker electrician applicants and must be documented as part of the application process.

The Journey Worker Electrician license is different from a contractor license. Hawaii’s requirements state that an electrician’s license does not allow a person to contract to perform electrical work. A contractor’s license is required for contracting activity. Students should understand the difference between being licensed as an individual electrician and operating as an electrical contractor.

Hawaii does not reciprocate with any jurisdiction for these electrician licenses. Applicants with out-of-state experience or licenses must still follow Hawaii’s application rules, submit required verification, and be qualified by the Board before testing.

Licensing Steps

North Dakota candidates begin by confirming that the Journeyman Electrician license is the correct license classification. The North Dakota State Electrical Board issues electrical licenses and reviews applicant qualifications before authorizing candidates to take the examination.

A practical licensing path begins with registering and working as an apprentice electrician under the supervision of a contracting master or master of record licensed electrician in a jurisdiction with similar licensing and inspection rules to North Dakota. Candidates should complete the required experience and apprentice electrician training, document qualifying work, submit the examination application and employment verification, receive Board approval, select an available exam date, take the examination, and complete the licensing process after passing.

The Board states that a Journeyman electrician must have completed 8,000 hours of experience, which may not be obtained in less than three years, while registered as an apprentice electrician. Up to 3,000 hours may apply under Class B electrician qualifications. The experience must be under the supervision of a contracting master or master of record licensed electrician in an area with similar licensing and inspection rules to North Dakota, and the applicant must have successfully completed apprentice electrician training.

The Board may grant 2,000 hours of credit for a graduate of a two-year or longer electrical school accepted by the Board. Practical experience consists of wiring for and installing electrical wiring, apparatus, and equipment. Additional experience credit may be allowed in areas such as repair work, fire alarm technology circuits or systems, process control circuits or power limited systems, and qualifying electrical construction experience gained in the armed forces.

After the Board approves an application, the applicant receives an invitation to take the examination. Exam Details

South Carolina journeyman-level electrician certification is connected to the CAGC SC Trades Certification Program. As of January 1, 2026, the CAGC Foundation oversees the trade certification process that was formerly managed through the Municipal Association of South Carolina. The CAGC SC Trade Certification card confirms that the cardholder has satisfied the experience and written examination qualifications required by the program for the level of certification indicated.

The CAGC trade certification card is not the same as a South Carolina Mechanical Contractors License or a South Carolina Residential Builders Commission Specialty Contractors License. Candidates who plan to perform commercial contracting work, residential specialty contracting work, or business operations should confirm whether they also need a license through the South Carolina Contractors Licensing Board or the South Carolina Residential Builders Commission.

Applicants for a new CAGC SC Trades Certification complete the application process, pay the application fee, and wait for review. Once approved, the applicant receives notification from PROV, the CAGC Foundation’s contracted examination provider. Applicants are responsible for scheduling their own exam date with PROV. Exams may be taken online or in person at an approved testing facility.

South Carolina also has residential electrical licensing through the South Carolina Residential Builders Commission. Residential Specialty Contractors taking the electrical technical examination are tested through the Commission’s examination program. The residential electrical technical examination is listed as a 60-question examination, and applicants must meet the passing score established by the Commission’s examination instructions. Residential candidates may also need to complete the Business Management and Law examination depending on the license path.

Journeyman-level electrical preparation should include general electrical knowledge, services, service equipment, feeders, branch circuits, conductors, wiring methods and materials, raceways, boxes, grounding and bonding, overcurrent protection, equipment for general use, motors, transformers, control devices, special occupancies, special equipment, special conditions, safety, and electrical calculations.

For CAGC SC Trades Certification, candidates complete the new certification application in full, submit the application fee, and wait for the application review. After approval, the candidate receives notification from PROV and schedules the examination. The candidate then takes the exam online or in person at an approved testing facility. If the candidate does not pass or allows the exam voucher to expire, the retesting process is handled through the program’s current retest instructions.

For residential electrical licensing, candidates follow the South Carolina Residential Builders Commission process. This may include meeting the Commission’s application, experience, and examination requirements, applying to the state, taking the required technical examination, completing any required business examination, and satisfying the licensing steps required before performing regulated residential electrical work.

For commercial electrical contracting, candidates should follow the South Carolina Contractors Licensing Board process. The contractor licensing path applies to commercial work and business operations that require a contractor license. Contractor applicants may need to meet separate classification, examination, financial, business, and license requirements.

Washington electrician certification is regulated by the Washington State Department of Labor & Industries.

What is the Washington 01 General Journey Level Electrician certificate?

The Washington 01 General Journey Level Electrician certificate is the broad journey level electrician credential that allows the holder to perform all types of electrical and telecommunications installations within the scope allowed by Washington law and rule.

Who administers the Washington electrician exam?

PSI administers Washington electrical certification examinations for the Washington State Department of Labor & Industries.

What sections are on the Washington 01 electrician exam?

What score is required to pass the Washington electrician exam?

Washington requires a score of 70% to pass the electrical examination.

Licensing Steps

Montana electrician licensing is handled through the Montana State Electrical Board. A candidate pursuing the Montana Master Electrician license should begin by confirming that the master electrician license is the correct credential for the work, supervision, planning, and responsibility they intend to perform.

A practical licensing path includes meeting the education or experience requirement, submitting the master electrician application to the Board, providing the required documentation, receiving Board approval for examination, scheduling the examination through PSI, passing the Master Electrician examination, and completing the licensing process through the Board.

Montana provides two primary qualification paths for the Master Electrician license by examination. One path is written evidence of being a graduate electrical engineer of an accredited college or university with a minimum of 2,000 hours of legally obtained practical electrical experience. The other path is third-party verification of at least 8,000 hours of legally obtained journeyman-level experience in planning, laying out, or supervising the installation and repair of wiring, apparatus, or equipment for electrical light, heat, and power. Montana’s checklist also notes that not more than 50 percent of the experience may be residential experience.

After the Board approves the application for examination, the applicant receives an admission letter and can schedule through PSI. Montana’s published exam information also includes retesting rules. After a first failure, a candidate may reschedule without a waiting period. After a second failure, a waiting period and approved electrical code seminar requirement apply. After three or more failures, the candidate must wait longer, submit a new application, and attend additional approved code seminars.

Licensing Steps

A practical Texas licensing path begins by confirming that the Master Electrician license is the correct license for the work and responsibility the candidate intends to perform. Texas requires a license for non-exempt electrical work, and electrical work must be performed through a licensed electrical contractor when required by law.

To apply for a Texas Master Electrician license, the applicant must have held a Journeyman Electrician license for at least two years. TDLR notes that Journeyman Industrial Electrician experience may not be used to qualify for a Master Electrician license. The applicant must also show completion of 12,000 hours of on-the-job training under the supervision of a Master Electrician licensed in Texas.

The applicant must obtain verification from each Master Electrician who supervised the qualifying work. The experience must be documented and signed by each supervisor on the required Experience Verification Form. If the applicant has held a municipal or regional master electrician license, the applicant may be able to verify on-the-job training for the years that the municipal or regional master license was held.

After preparing the experience documentation, the applicant submits the Master Electrician License Application Form and application fee to TDLR. The initial Texas Master Electrician application is submitted by mail. After the completed application has been received and verified, TDLR notifies the applicant of approval to take the licensing examination.

Once approved for testing, the candidate schedules the examination through PSI. The Texas Master Electrician exam includes the NEC Knowledge Portion and the Calculations Portion, and both portions must be passed with a minimum score of 70 percent. After the examination is completed, PSI sends results to TDLR electronically. The candidate does not need to send exam results to TDLR separately.

After the candidate satisfies the examination and remaining licensing requirements, TDLR completes the license process. Texas electrician licenses are valid for one year from the date of issuance and must be renewed annually. Renewal is completed through TDLR, and licensees should follow the current continuing education and renewal rules that apply to their license category.

Exam Details

Utah electrician licensing is handled through the Utah Division of Professional Licensing under the Utah Department of Commerce. Utah has several electrician license classifications, including Apprentice, Journeyman, Master, Residential Journeyman, and Residential Master. Candidates pursuing the Utah Master Electrician license must meet the education and experience path required for the classification and pass the required examinations.

Utah’s electrical licensing examinations are administered through Prov. Beginning August 1, 2025, Utah changed the electrician licensing examination structure. Master Electrician candidates no longer take separate theory and code exams. Instead, Master Electrician candidates take the Utah Master Electrician Law and Rules examination. Master Electrician candidates must also pass the Utah Electrician Practical Exam unless the practical exam was previously passed as part of earning a Utah Journeyman Electrician license.

The Utah Master Electrician Rule and Laws examination is listed with 80 questions, 240 minutes of testing time, and a required passing score of 75 percent. The content outline includes communications systems, conductors and cables, the Utah Construction Trades Licensing Act, current, resistance, voltage drop, definitions and general requirements, the DOPL Licensing Act, the Electricians Licensing Act Rule, general DOPL licensing rules, grounding and bonding, lighting and general-use equipment, motors and controllers, NFPA 70E, overcurrent protection, raceways and enclosures, services, feeders, branch circuits, special conditions, special occupancies and equipment, Utah health and safety material, Utah labor code material, Utah occupational health and safety material, and Utah NEC amendments.

The Utah Electrician Practical Exam is a hands-on examination listed with 6 tasks and 110 minutes of testing time. The practical exam subjects include torque setting, transformer termination, conduit bending, commercial motor control using a ladder diagram, 4-way and 3-way switch wiring, and schematic reading and wiring. Candidates who previously passed the Utah Electrician Practical Exam when earning a Journeyman license are not required to retake that practical exam for the Master Electrician license.

Open Book Test

The Utah Master Electrician Law and Rules examination is an open book examination. Open book testing does not make the exam easy. It means candidates must know how to use approved references efficiently, read code and rule language carefully, understand table notes and exceptions, and apply requirements under time pressure.

Utah’s exam reference rules allow candidates to use listed reference books during theory or code examinations. Current and previous year code books are permitted for use during the exam. The bulletin encourages candidates to prepare testing materials by highlighting text or placing permanent tabs on important pages. Candidates must follow the exam provider’s reference rules for exact titles, editions, permanent tabs, highlighting, underlining, handwritten notes, added documents, stickers, and marking in books during the exam.

Reference rules are strict. Moveable tabs such as repositionable tabs or Post-it notes are not permitted. Books may have highlighting and underlining in pen, but candidates may not mark in books during the test. Handwritten notes are not allowed in any portion of a reference book unless authorized by the licensing or certifying jurisdiction. Other documents, formula sheets, indexes, stickers, or attached items may not be added, glued, or taped into a reference book unless permitted by the exam details.

Licensing Steps

A practical Utah licensing path begins by confirming that the Master Electrician license is the correct classification for the candidate’s goal. Utah’s Master Electrician classification is a higher-level individual electrical license, and candidates should understand the difference between an individual electrician license and any separate contractor or business licensing requirements that may apply to electrical contracting activity.

Utah applicants for the Master Electrician license may qualify through one of several paths. One path requires 8,000 hours of experience as a licensed Journeyman Electrician, passing the Utah Master Electrician Law and Rule exam, and passing the Utah Electrician Practical Exam unless the practical exam was previously passed as a Journeyman. Another path requires a bachelor’s or master’s degree in an electrical engineering program accredited by EAC/ABET, 2,000 hours of work experience as a licensed Apprentice Electrician, and the required exams. Another path requires an associate degree in applied science from an electrical trade school course of study, 4,000 hours of work experience as a licensed Journeyman Electrician, and the required exams.

Utah does not require preapproval before testing for the electrician exams. Candidates register and schedule examinations through Prov and must self-certify under penalty of perjury that they meet the necessary exam eligibility requirements before beginning the exam. Effective January 19, 2026, first-time candidates registering for licensing exams with Prov must submit the Verification of Electrician Experience form directly to Prov by electronically attaching it to the exam registration.

After meeting the testing path and passing the required examination components, the candidate completes the license application process through Utah DOPL. Utah provides online, manual, and in-person application options. Applicants should prepare required experience documentation, education documentation when applicable, exam results, personal identification information, and any other required application materials.
